title: What Is an Externship? How They Work & Why You Need One | Extern
summary: An externship is a short-term, project-based professional experience with a real company. Learn how externships work, what you gain, and why students rate them 4.8/5.
body_text: "You need an internship to land a full-time job!" ‍ "What are you going to put on your resume?" ‍ “You’re about to graduate in the worst economy in two decades.” Sound familiar? If you’re a student, chances are you’ve heard some version of this way too many times. The problem? Landing an internship is harder than ever. And without experience, breaking into your dream career can feel next to impossible. But what if there was another way to gain real-world experience, build job-ready skills, and make your resume stand out—without going through the ultra-competitive internship application cycle? Enter the Externship. Externships provide students with flexible, remote, and structured work experiences, where you contribute to real business projects, receive mentorship, and develop career skills. Whether you’re exploring career options, strengthening your resume, or trying to get your foot in the door with top employers, Externships offer a powerful alternative. ‍ What is an Externship? Simply put, an Externship is remote work experience delivered in the format of a class. It is a structured, short-term, virtual experience that blends academic learning with real-world business projects. Unlike internships, which typically require full-time commitments, Externships last 8-12 weeks with just 10 hours per week, making them ideal for students who need flexibility. Externships are designed to be completed alongside coursework or even another internship, allowing students to test-drive multiple career paths and industries before committing to a specific job or graduate program. At Extern, students can choose from a range of Externships in industries like finance, consulting, strategy, product and marketing—all with mentorship and training built-in. ‍ Why Should I do an Externship? Getting hired without prior experience is not just hard, it’s often impossible: The job market has never been more competitive for early talent. Nearly every internship requires some level of work experience and, shockingly, nearly 40% of “entry-level jobs” on LinkedIn now require 3+ years of experience. ‍ Certifications only get you halfway there: That’s because employers want to see that you not only learned useful skills, but that you actually have experience applying them to real work. ‍ Externships are guaranteed professional experience: At Extern, we believe there is nothing more valuable for a career than gaining professional experience as a form of education. Unlike traditional internships (which often require endless applications and ghosting from recruiters), once you’re accepted as an Extern member, you can choose whatever externship you want to do, at any time—no more resume black holes, no more playing the waiting game. ‍ ‍ Build a standout resume (even if you’re not “perfectly aligned”): Breaking into your dream career is tough, especially if your background doesn’t perfectly fit the traditional mold. But guess what? That shouldn’t hold you back. Externships let you gain real-world experience in any industry, no matter your major, GPA, or school. Want to be a venture capitalist but majoring in sociology? No problem. Looking to break into tech with a marketing degree? Go for it. Externships give you the freedom to build the experience you need—not just the experience your resume currently shows. ‍ Explore careers before you commit: It’s frustrating when you finally land an internship, only to realize… you don’t even like the field. But by then, you’ve already spent months applying and wasted an entire summer. With externships, you don’t have to commit long-term before figuring out what’s right for you. They’re shorter, more flexible, and available year-round, so by the time summer rolls around, you’ll already know exactly which industry you want to intern in. ‍ Differentiate yourself in a crowded job market: Applying to jobs feels like competing in the Hunger Games. Everyone has a similar resume, similar coursework, and the same list of extracurriculars. So how do you stand out? Unique experiences like externships set you apart. They give you compelling stories to tell in interviews and prove that your skills are transferable across industries. ‍ Hear from former extern Thomas Heslop of Howard University “I'm a pre-med student that did a remote Externship with a VC firm. It wasn’t because I wanted to hang up my future white coat! The traditional road to medicine is a straightforward path, but I wanted to use my summer to explore the business world. The experience taught me a lot. I built on my Excel skills and pitch creation, both of which are transferable skills that are useful in any industry." ‍ Externships = a low-pressure way to gain real-world experience, explore career options, and build a resume that actually gets noticed. So why wait? ‍ What an Externship is NOT: Common Misconceptions We hear these misconceptions all the time, so we’re here to set the record straight. To clear things up, here’s what an Externship is NOT : ❌ Externships are NOT case studies or simulations. Every Externship is a real business project, often designed to generate insights for an actual company. ❌ Externships are NOT busy work. Externs receive structured training and apply job-ready skills to meaningful projects. ❌ Externships are NOT job shadowing. Instead of watching others work, Externs actively participate in business projects and problem-solving. ❌ Externships are NOT long-term commitments. They’re designed to be short, flexible, and remote, making them accessible for students with busy schedules. ❌ Externships are NOT internships. While they provide real professional experience, externships are different from internships that are hosted directly by companies. See below for the fill list of the differences! However, some Externships are Internship-Track , meaning top performers may be considered for paid internships or full-time roles directly with the host company. ‍ Externship vs. Internship: Which One is Right for You? While both Externships and internships provide valuable experience, they cater to different needs: ‍ Feature Internship Externship Time Commitment Full-time 10–15 hours/week Duration Typically a full summer 6–12 weeks, available year-round Competitiveness Highly selective, limited spots More accessible, flexible enrollment Mentorship Varies by company Structured mentorship & training Access Companies choose interns based on applications and interviews Students choose any available Externship they want to do after being accepted as an Extern member Work Environment In-person or remote Fully remote Career Exploration High-commitment option focused on a single role Designed as short, flexible programs so students can explore multiple industries and roles before making longer-term career commitments ‍ What is the Purpose of an Externship? Think of an Externship as a sneak peek into your future career, but with training wheels. It's your golden ticket to dive into real projects, giving you a front-row seat to what life looks like in your dream career. It's about taking all that theory you've crammed into your brain and applying it to the real world, boosting your skills, and getting a feel for different career paths. Forget the old-school classroom vibe; an Externship is your chance to test-drive potential jobs and employers, making sure you're building the skills that matter in the real world. It's all about making your leap into the professional world smoother and smarter. ‍ Externships bridge the gap between academic learning and real-world work experience. Here’s why they’re becoming essential for students: ✅ Explore Careers Before Committing – Think professional playground: students try different industries and roles without the long-term commitment of an internship. ✅ Gain Real-World Experience – Work on actual business problems, not just theoretical exercises. ✅ Build Job-Ready Skills – Learn to analyze data, develop marketing strategies, conduct research, and more. ✅ Expand Your Network – Connect with mentors, industry professionals, and company decision-makers. ✅ Boost Your Resume – Showcase tangible experience that sets you apart from other applicants. ‍ The Externship Experience at Extern At Extern, our mission is to make real professional experience accessible to anyone, anywhere. More than 17,000 students register for externships each semester, representing 100+ different majors — from finance and data science to sociology and art history. Extern partners with Fortune 500 companies, startups, and industry leaders — including Amazon, Beats by Dre, HP, Pfizer, TikTok, National Geographic, and PwC — to offer structured Externships in consulting, marketing, product management, finance, gaming, healthcare, and more. Each Externship includes: ✔️ A structured curriculum with training modules ✔️ Real-world business projects from exciting brands ✔️ Mentorship from industry experts ✔️ Career-development resources, workshops and webinars ✔️ Networking opportunities with executives and peers ✔️ Flexible scheduling that fits around your coursework ‍ Here’s what one extern had to say about their experience: ‍ ‍ "The Externship expanded my knowledge and provided me with valuable talking points in job interviews. Thanks to the skills I gained, I secured two internships during my undergrad!" – Jannah Shakil, North Carolina State University ‍ Are Externships Worth It? 100% YES. Externships are the perfect way to gain work experience without the stress of traditional internship applications. 📌 In our post-program survey of 1,800+ students, 93% rated their externship experience positively — with more than half selecting "Very Satisfied". 📌 Internship-Track Externships give students a direct path to paid internships with top employers like Amazon, Beats by Dre, and PwC. 📌 Extern's Net Promoter Score is +51, meaning nearly 6 in 10 students would actively recommend the experience to a friend. 📌 In a product-market fit survey, 56% of students said they'd be "very disappointed" if Extern didn't exist — well above the 40% benchmark for strong product-market fit. ‍ Can an Externship Help You Get Hired? Externships are one of the best ways to break into competitive fields. Employers today often require 3+ years of experience for "entry-level" jobs—creating a frustrating catch-22 for students. Externships help break that cycle by giving students real, project-based work experience before they even apply for an internship or job. In fact, many students use their Externship experience to: 📌 Secure internships and full-time roles at top firms 📌 Impress recruiters with real-world projects 📌 Get hired at the Externship host company 📌 Strengthen applications for graduate programs ‍ Hear from former extern Richard Min! ‍ ‍ “ I found Extern because I overheard students in the library talking about how cool it was! I looked it up on my laptop, applied, and a month later was doing a venture capital externship. That single moment led to multiple externships and opened up Extern's professional network to me. It directly helped me land two internships and incredible connections in venture capital. And I'm now an incoming Summer Analyst at J.P. Morgan! ” - Richard Min, LSE ‍ “I credit the externship as the sole reason I was hired to intern at AT&T. I had never heard of the AT&T internship program and would never even have applied to it if I hadn’t gone through the externship. It allowed me to develop my skills, showcase my work and ultimately stand out so I was awarded the fantastic opportunity to interview the CEO of AT&T!” ‍ - Tori Nguyen, Virginia Commonwealth University ‍ “"During my venture capital externship, I learned how to use industry-standard metrics and tools like SQL and Tableau to determine startup success potential. This opportunity helped me stand out as a candidate and opened new doors for me - including offers from EY and Accenture" ‍ - Maisa Mirza, The University of Texas at Dallas ‍ ‍ Who Can Do An Externship? Anyone. Seriously. Externships are designed for students from all majors, backgrounds, and levels of experience. Unlike internships that often require years of prior experience (yes, even for “entry-level” roles—wild, right?), externships welcome students who are just starting their career journeys. ‍ ‍ ✔️ Freshman testing the waters? Perfect. Externships help you explore different fields before committing to an internship. ✔️ Sophomore or junior looking for hands-on experience? Gain resume-boosting skills that make you stand out. ✔️ Senior or just graduated? The pressure is on and if the right internships or roles just aren’t happening, give your resume a boost with an Externship that will make you more marketable to recruiters. ✔️ Switching your major? No problem. Externships help you break into a new field, so you can “catch up” and snag the roles you want, even if your past experience doesn’t match the job descriptions you’re applying to. No GPA cutoffs. No restrictions based on what school you attend. Just real opportunities to gain experience that matters. ‍ ‍ "My Externship really changed my career trajectory. It taught me that I definitely want to pursue a career in the banking industry. I even made the decision to switch my major to Economics to better align with this goal! As students, we often chase after Fortune 500 work experiences, but the intimate experience of getting to work with a startup can actually really help you learn a lot and level up what you can bring to the table. The externship helped me develop hard skills, but also soft skills like communication and presentation." - Diego Juarez, now an analyst at J.P. Morgan Chase & Co ‍ What Skills Can I Learn at an Externship? While the skills you gain depend on the specific externship you choose, our extern alumni consistently highlight these game-changing skills as some of the most valuable takeaways from their experience: Data Skills: Learn how to clean, analyze, and visualize large datasets using industry-standard tools. Whether you're working in marketing, finance, or tech, understanding data is a must-have skill for making informed decisions. Storytelling & Presentation Skills: No matter what career path you take, being able to distill complex information into a clear, compelling story is essential. You'll gain experience in crafting impactful presentations, structuring data-driven narratives, and communicating your insights effectively to decision-makers. Technical Skills (SQL, Python & More): Whether you're querying databases with SQL, automating tasks with Python, or exploring coding basics, externships give you hands-on exposure to technical skills that impress employers in nearly every industry. Critical Thinking & Problem-Solving: Every externship challenges you to analyze real-world problems and propose solutions. You’ll develop the ability to think strategically, work through challenges, and adapt quickly—skills that are invaluable in any job. AI Skills & Emerging Tech: The future of work is AI-driven, and externships give you the chance to stay ahead. You’ll learn how to leverage AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gamma to build chatbots, create next-level presentations, and analyze data faster—giving you a huge competitive edge in the hiring market. Professional Development Skills: Externships also help you polish your LinkedIn profile, craft a standout resume, and build a personal brand that makes employers take notice. Plus, you’ll develop networking skills that will help you build meaningful industry connections. Familiarity with Workplace Tools: Get comfortable using Slack, Zoom, Notion, Asana, and other essential tools that modern companies rely on every day. By the time you start an internship or full-time job, you’ll already know the ropes. By the end of your externship, you won’t just list skills on your resume—you’ll have real projects and experiences to back them up. 🚀 ‍ ‍ “Less than two months after my externship, I landed a junior year internship with Goldman Sachs. I talked a lot about the project we worked on during the externship—how we had to check in on different points of the work, and how that really built my confidence. I mentioned this in all my interviews, and it definitely helped. I also had an HR internship this summer, and they noticed my confidence. I credit that to the experience I had earlier in the year with Extern.” ‍ - Bintou Majula Drammeh, now interns at Goldman Sachs ‍ Examples of Externships at Extern Extern collaborates with industry leaders to design high-impact, real-world projects for students. This Externship is your chance to tackle these challenges head-on. Over 6 weeks, you’ll research real workflows, uncover pain points, and design smarter systems to improve patient experiences. body_text: Uses in Cutting Metal and Pipes Cutting metal and pipes represents a primary function for the angle grinder in plumbing and construction. The tool utilizes thin abrasive cutoff wheels (1 millimeter to 3 millimeters thick) to penetrate iron and steel. Operators mark the cut line on the pipe before applying the rotating disc. The high speed rotation allows the abrasive to remove material through microscopic shearing and abrasion. Pipe diameters from 0.5 inches to 4 inches are easily managed with a standard 4.5 inch grinder. Large diameter pipes (6 inches to 10 inches) require a 7 inch or 9 inch model. The tool provides a faster alternative to hacksaws or reciprocating saws. Sparks fly from the contact point as the disc removes material. The cut edge often requires deburring with a grinding disc after the separation. Accuracy depends on the steady hand of the operator. Portable units allow for cutting in trenches or overhead positions. The process generates significant heat in the workpiece. Uses in Grinding and Smoothing Welds and Surfaces Grinding and smoothing welds involve the removal of surface irregularities and excess material in metal fabrication. Welders often leave excess bead material (slag and overfill) after joining metal plates. The angle grinder uses a thick grinding disc (6 millimeters) to level the surface. The abrasive action blends the weld into the surrounding base metal. Smoothing ensures a professional appearance and prepares the metal for painting. Surface preparation requires the disc to be held at an angle from 15 degrees to 30 degrees. Heavy pressure removes material quickly while light pressure provides a smoother finish. Flap discs (layered sandpaper) are used for finer smoothing tasks. Grit sizes for flap discs range from 40 to 120. The process reveals surface-breaking defects (porosity or cracks) in the weld. Grinding also removes mill scale from hot rolled steel. The tool provides a surface finish that reduces stress concentrations to improve fatigue life. Consistent movement prevents the creation of deep gouges in the metal. Uses in Polishing and Finishing Materials Polishing and finishing materials involve using the angle grinder at lower speeds with specialized attachments. Buffing pads, felt wheels, and polishing bonnets attach to the spindle. The process enhances the aesthetic quality of stainless steel, stone, and automotive paint. Polishing compounds (pastes and waxes) are applied to the surface to reduce friction. Variable speed grinders are recommended for the task to prevent burning the material. Speeds from 2,000 to 4,000 RPM provide the best results for finishing. Higher speeds cause the polishing compound to sling off the disc. The operator moves the tool in circular patterns to achieve a uniform shine. Polishing stainless steel removes scratches and creates a mirror finish. Masonry professionals use diamond polishing pads to finish granite countertops. Grit sequences for stone polishing range from 50 to 3,000. The final result depends on the gradual progression through finer abrasives. Finishing tasks requires a light touch to avoid damaging the surface. Uses in Removing Rust and Paint Removing rust and paint involves the use of wire brushes and stripping discs on an angle grinder. Corrosion weakens metal structures and prevents proper coating adhesion. Wire cup brushes feature stiff steel or brass bristles that scrape away iron oxide. The high speed rotation allows the bristles to sweep effectively across surface pits and shallow irregularities. Stripping discs (poly-fiber) remove paint without gouging the underlying metal. The discs operate effectively on flat surfaces and curved profiles. Rust removal is a standard step in automotive restoration and bridge maintenance. The process produces a large amount of dust and debris. Operators must wear respirators to avoid inhaling paint particles. Heat generation is lower compared to grinding with abrasive discs. The tool removes layers of powder coatings and non-toxic paint; however, lead-based paint must not be ground as it creates hazardous airborne particles. Surface preparation with an angle grinder extends the life of new paint jobs. The method is faster than manual wire brushing or sanding. Wire wheels come in diameters from 3 inches to 5 inches. Uses in Sharpening Tools and Blades Sharpening tools and blades requires a steady hand and a fine grit grinding disc. Lawnmower blades, axes, and garden shears lose their edges through use. The angle grinder restores the bevel by removing a small amount of metal. The operator secures the blade in a vise before sharpening. The disc is held at the original factory angle (20 degrees to 45 degrees). Light passes prevent the metal from overheating and losing its temper. Bluing of the metal indicates excessive heat, which softens the edge. Flap discs with 80 or 120 grit provide a sharp and smooth finish. The tool provides a quick way to repair nicks in heavy equipment blades. High-accuracy sharpening for chisels or knives usually requires a slow-speed wet stone or whetstone. The angle grinder is preferred for large outdoor tools. Sharpening increases the efficiency of the cutting tools. The process requires frequent checking of the edge for sharpness. Proper balance must be maintained when sharpening lawnmower blades. How Do Other Grinding Machines Compare To Angle Grinders? Other grinding machines are usually stationary and more specialized than angle grinders. Precision and stability distinguish industrial equipment from handheld units. Bench grinders feature two wheels mounted on a fixed motor shaft for tool sharpening. Surface grinders use a magnetic chuck to hold workpieces for high tolerance finishing. Cylindrical grinders process the outside of rods with extreme accuracy. The angle grinder provides portability at the expense of precision. Stationary machines offer rigid support to ensure perfectly flat or round results. Handheld units depend on the stability of the user's arms. Industrial grinders handle larger volumes of material in production environments. Tool and cutter grinders specialize in complex geometries for drill bits. The portability of the angle grinder makes the tool suitable for repair work on existing structures. Accuracy for stationary machines reaches tolerances of [0.001 to 0.002] inches. Handheld grinding results vary by several millimeters. Professionals choose Grinding Machines based on the required tolerance. What are the Most Common Types of Grinding Machines Used Today? The most common types of grinding machines used today are listed below. Surface Grinding Machine : Surface grinding machine creates flat, smooth finishes by moving a rotating wheel across a workpiece fixed on a table. Precision work depends on controlled passes that remove minimal material while maintaining tight tolerances (tooling plates, machine bases). Surface grinding machine supports finishing operations where flatness and surface quality define performance. Cylindrical Grinding Machine : A cylindrical grinding machine shapes round components through rotation along a central axis between centers or chucks. Machining processes rely on cylindrical grinding machines for external diameters that demand accuracy and consistent surface finish (shafts, spindles). Cylindrical grinding machine supports both rough grinding and fine finishing stages. Centerless Grinding Machine : A centerless grinding machine removes material without clamping the workpiece, using a regulating wheel and support blade to control rotation and position. High-output production lines depend on a centerless grinding machine for uniform sizing and fast throughput (metal rods, precision pins). A centerless grinding machine maintains a consistent diameter across large batches without repositioning. Tool and Cutter Grinding Machine : The tool and cutter grinding machine restores and reshapes cutting tools through controlled grinding angles and profiles. Workshops maintain tool performance by using a tool and cutter grinding machine for reconditioning worn edges (end mills, drill bits). The tool and cutter grinding machine supports custom tool geometry for specialized machining tasks. Bench Grinding Machine : A bench grinding machine handles general-purpose grinding with dual wheels mounted on a stationary frame. Maintenance work uses a bench grinding machine for sharpening, cleaning, and edge preparation (chisels, metal edges). Bench grinding machine supports quick adjustments and small-scale material removal tasks. Angle Grinding Machine : The angle grinding machine operates as a handheld unit designed for mobility and versatility in cutting and grinding. Fabrication and construction tasks rely on an angle grinding machine for flexible operations across metal and masonry surfaces (pipe cutting, weld smoothing). Angle grinding machine adapts to different discs for multiple surface treatments. Internal Grinding Machine : An internal grinding machine finishes internal diameters through precise abrasive contact inside bores and holes. Precision engineering tasks depend on an internal grinding machine for smooth internal surfaces and accurate sizing (bearing interiors, cylindrical cavities). An internal grinding machine ensures dimensional accuracy in enclosed geometries. Can Angle Grinder Attachments Replace Some Grinding Machines? Yes, angle grinder attachments can perform tasks similar to grinding machines. Stands and guides convert the handheld tool into a semi-stationary device. A miter stand allows the grinder to perform straight cuts like a chop saw. Sanding pads permit the tool to act as a disk sander for wood or metal. The attachments increase the versatility of the base unit. Industrial grinding machines provide levels of precision that attachments cannot match. Rigid frames on stationary machines prevent the deflection found in handheld tools. Motor power on industrial units exceeds the capacity of small angle grinders. Attachments serve the needs of hobbyists and small workshops. Large scale manufacturing requires the consistency of dedicated machines. The cost of a stand ranges from [$30 to $300]. Precision remains the primary factor in choosing a dedicated machine. Functional overlaps exist for light duty tasks. The tool requires careful setup for accurate results. How Is Angle Milling Related to Angle Grinder Uses? Angle milling involves machining at an angle, while angle grinders are mainly used for cutting or grinding surfaces. The milling process utilizes a multi-point cutting tool on a milling machine. The machine head or the table tilts to create precise angular features (chamfers or dovetails). Angle grinders remove material through abrasive friction without specific dimensional control. Milling produces a finished surface with exact measurements and a high quality finish. The angle grinder is a roughing tool for general material removal. Operators use the grinder for beveling plate edges before welding. The grinder lacks the lead screws and dials found on a mill. Milling machines operate at speeds ranging from 500 to over 20,000 RPM. Accuracy for milling reaches [0.0001 to 0.002] inches. Handheld grinding is used when tolerances are wide. Precision manufacturing relies on Angle Milling for complex parts. How does Angle Milling Compare to Typical Angle Grinder Tasks? Angle milling is more precise than typical angle grinder tasks. Milling involves controlled machining with a rigid setup. The workpiece is clamped to a table to eliminate movement. Typical grinder tasks involve freehand operation with the tool held by the user. Milling tools have defined cutting edges that produce chips. Grinder discs use abrasive grains that produce microscopic chips (swarf) and sparks. The finish from a milling cutter is smooth and regular. Grinding leaves a scratched surface that requires further finishing. Milling machines can remove large amounts of material in a single pass. Angle grinders require multiple passes to achieve deep cuts. The setup time for milling is longer than for grinding. Grinding is faster for simple cutoff or cleanup jobs. Precision and speed are the main trade-offs. Milling requires specialized training for safe operation. The choice of method depends on the project requirements. Can an Angle Grinder Be Used for Simple Angle Milling Jobs? An angle grinder cannot be used for simple angle milling jobs requiring high accuracy. The tool lacks the rigid constraints needed to maintain a constant angle. Manual guidance leads to variations in the slope of the cut. Milling requires the tool to move along a fixed axis. The angle grinder moves in any direction dictated by the hand of the user. Simple beveling is possible for weld preparation. The result will not meet the standards of a machined chamfer. Specialized jigs for grinders can improve the consistency of the angle. These jigs do not provide the stability of a 2,000 pound milling machine. The abrasive disc wears down during use, changing the depth of the cut. Carbide end mills in a machine maintain their dimensions much longer. The grinder is a tool for fabrication rather than precision machining. Surface finishes from a grinder are rougher than milled surfaces. Accuracy remains the defining difference between the two methods. How does Centerless Grinding Differ From Angle Grinder Applications? Centerless grinding differs by supporting the workpiece without centers or a chuck. The process uses two wheels (a grinding wheel and a regulating wheel) to hold the part. A work rest blade supports the workpiece from below as it passes through the wheels. Angle grinders require the operator to hold the tool and the part manually. Centerless grinding is an automated industrial process for high volume production. Handheld grinding is a manual process for individual pieces or on-site work. Precision in centerless systems reaches tolerances of [0.0001] inches. Angle grinders produce results with tolerances of [0.02 to 0.04] inches. The industrial process handles thousands of parts per hour. Handheld units are used for one-off modifications and repairs. Roundness and straightness are guaranteed by the centerless machine. Portable grinders are used for shaping and smoothing. Industrial manufacturing depends on Centerless Grinding for pins and rollers. What Makes Centerless Grinding Different From Handheld Grinding? Centerless grinding is a precise and automated process, while handheld grinding is manual and less controlled. The machine controls the feed rate and the pressure applied to the part. Handheld grinding depends on the physical strength and skill of the worker. Consistency is the hallmark of the centerless method. Every part produced by the machine matches the previous one. Handheld results vary from part to part. Automation in centerless grinding reduces the risk of human error. Safety guards on machines are more comprehensive than those on portable tools. The workpiece in centerless grinding is always supported at three points. Portable grinding often involves unsupported parts or simple vises. Material removal rates are higher and more consistent in the automated process. Cooling systems on machines allow for heavy grinding without burning the part. Portable grinders typically rely on air cooling and manual thermal management. The two methods serve different ends of the manufacturing spectrum. Can an Angle Grinder Achieve Similar Results to Centerless Grinding? An angle grinder cannot achieve similar results to centerless grinding. The levels of precision and roundness produced by a machine are impossible to replicate by hand. Centerless grinding creates parts with micron-level accuracy. Handheld grinding is limited by the visual and tactile feedback of the operator. The absence of a rigid support system for the part prevents perfect roundness. Flat spots and ridges are common in handheld work. Angle grinders are intended for material removal rather than geometric correction. Achieving a constant diameter over a long rod is not possible with a portable tool. The handheld nature of the grinder lacks the rigid support system and constrained motion required for precision. Industrial machines use wheels up to 24 inches in diameter. The speed of production also differs by several orders of magnitude. The portable tool is used for deburring the ends of rods ground in a machine. Accuracy and repeatability remain exclusive to the automated equipment. What Safety Precautions Are Required When Using an Angle Grinder? Safety Precautions required when using an angle grinder are listed below. Wear Protective Gear : Operators protect their eyes, face, hands, and hearing through proper equipment before starting any task. Safety goggles and face shields block flying fragments, while gloves protect hands from heat and sharp edges. Hearing protection reduces exposure to continuous high noise levels during extended operation (goggles, face shield, gloves, earplugs, respirator). Inspect the Grinder and Disc : Operators examine the grinder body, guard, spindle, and disc condition before use. Cracks, chips, an imbalance, or an expired shelf life for the disc increase the chance of sudden breakage at high speed. Secure mounting and proper tightening prevent disc movement during rotation (cracked disc, loose flange). Secure the Workpiece : Operators fix the material using clamps or a vise to prevent shifting during cutting or grinding. Stable positioning improves control and reduces sudden movement that leads to kickback. Fixed workpieces support straight cuts and consistent grinding pressure (bench vise, locking clamps). Use the Correct Disc Type : Operators select discs based on material and task to avoid excessive strain on the grinder. Cutting discs handle thin, straight cuts, while grinding wheels remove material from surfaces and welds. Proper selection, including matching the disc RPM to the grinder speed, extends disc life and maintains safe operation (metal cutting disc, flap disc for smoothing). Maintain Proper Grip and Position : Operators hold the grinder firmly with both hands and maintain a balanced stance during operation. Strong grip control keeps the disc aligned with the work surface and reduces the chance of slipping. Body positioning away from the disc path limits exposure to debris and sparks (two-hand grip, stable footing). Control Sparks and Direction : Operators direct sparks away from the body, nearby workers, and flammable materials in the workspace. Controlled spark flow reduces fire hazards and prevents burns during prolonged use. Clear surroundings eliminate ignition risks from flying hot particles (spark direction away from the operator and flammables, cleared workspace). Allow the Disc to Reach Full Speed : Operators start the grinder and wait until the disc reaches full rotational speed before contacting the material. Full speed stabilizes the disc and reduces vibration during initial contact. Gradual engagement prevents sudden jerks that lead to loss of control. Disconnect Power Before Adjustments : Operators turn off and disconnect the grinder before changing discs or performing maintenance. Power isolation removes the risk of accidental startup during handling. Safe handling during adjustments protects hands and prevents unexpected movement (disc replacement, cleaning procedures). What Protective Gear Should Be Worn During Operation? Protective gears be worn during operation is listed below. Safety Goggles : Operators shield their eyes from high-velocity metal fragments, dust, and abrasive particles produced during disc contact. Sealed designs block entry from the sides and maintain clear vision during continuous work (impact-rated lenses, wraparound fit). Face Shield : Operators cover the entire face to guard against larger debris and direct spark streams. Full-face coverage adds a secondary layer over goggles and reduces facial injury during aggressive cutting or grinding (clear visor, extended chin protection). Protective Gloves : Operators protect their hands from sharp edges, heat buildup, and vibration during prolonged use. Reinforced gloves improve grip control and protect against sparks, heat buildup, and vibration during prolonged use (cut-resistant material, padded grip zones). Hearing Protection : Operators reduce exposure to sustained noise levels generated by high-speed motors and abrasive contact. Consistent use of earplugs or earmuffs lowers the risk of long-term hearing damage during repeated operation (foam earplugs, over-ear protection). Protective Clothing : Operators wear long sleeves and thick materials to shield skin from sparks and debris. Close-fitting clothing prevents loose fabric from catching in the rotating disc or spindle (long-sleeve workwear, heavy-duty fabric). Steel-Toe Boots : Operators protect their feet from falling tools, metal pieces, and heavy work materials. Reinforced toe caps and slip-resistant soles support stable footing in workshop and construction environments (steel-toe protection, anti-slip base). Respiratory Mask : Operators filter airborne dust, metal particles, and debris generated during grinding processes. Respiratory protection improves air quality exposure in enclosed or high-dust environments (dust mask, particulate respirator). Is Wearing Safety Goggles Necessary When Using an Angle Grinder? Yes, wearing safety goggles is necessary when using an angle grinder. The tool produces a stream of hot sparks and abrasive particles. The fragments travel at high velocities and cause permanent eye damage. Standard glasses do not provide enough side protection. Safety goggles must meet the ANSI Z87.1 standard for impact resistance. Debris bounces off walls and enters the eyes from any angle. The risk of disc breakage makes eye protection a critical requirement. A shattered disc release fragments at speeds over 100 miles per hour. Eye injuries are among the most common accidents in metalworking shops. Goggles prevent dust from causing irritation and inflammation. The cost of a pair of goggles ranges from [$5 to $20]. Vision loss is a life-altering consequence of neglecting safety. PPE is the first line of defense in the workshop. Constant use ensures safety throughout the duration of the project. Eyes remain vulnerable to microscopic steel slivers. Staff will demonstrate temperature differentials using props, such as hot coffee and cold ice, to illustrate the precision and speed of MSAI Connect under realistic conditions. Such developments can change how reliability teams detect issues, respond to risk, and ultimately protect uptime across critical operations." The Reliability Conference draws more than 1,000 maintenance, reliability and asset management professionals annually. Based on 2025 attendee data, 69 percent expected to increase reliability and asset management spending within 24 months, and 63 percent of attendees operated under a formal digital transformation mandate. title: Digital adoption platforms in 2026: 10 tools, sorted by who they're for
summary: An honest 2026 read on the digital adoption platform category from a vendor inside it. Six commercial tools, four open-source alternatives, and where each one actually fits.
body_text: Digital adoption platforms layer guidance directly into a product so users can get to value without leaving the app. In 2026 the category has split: agent-based systems that learn the product on their own, no-code onboarding kits for SaaS, and enterprise overlay tools that have barely evolved in a decade. Below is how the ten we get asked about compare, sorted by which slice they're actually for. What is a digital adoption platform? A digital adoption platform (DAP) is software that layers in-product guidance directly into an application, so users can complete tasks without leaving the product or filing a support ticket. The category covers tours, tooltips, checklists, in-app messages, surveys, and increasingly AI agents. It started a decade ago as a pragmatic answer to a specific problem: software was getting more complicated than the help center could keep up with, and a generation of tools showed up to plug that gap. A decade later, the category has split. Some of the tools are full enterprise change-management suites. Some are lightweight onboarding kits a marketing team installs in an afternoon. A few have rebuilt themselves as AI agents because the assumption underneath the original product (you write the content, we place it in the right spot) doesn't hold the way it used to. This is the honest version of how the ten DAPs we get asked about compare in 2026: six commercial platforms, four open-source alternatives. We make one of them. We'll be upfront about where it fits and where it doesn't. 1. Frigade We make this one and we're listing it first because it's the only tool in the category that doesn't ask you to author the guidance. Every other tool below assumes someone on your team writes the tour, attaches it to the right DOM nodes, and re-authors it the next time the product changes. Frigade Assistant deploys an AI agent that learns your product the same way a new hire would: by actually using it. It learns your workflows, reads your help docs, maps the spots where users get stuck, and builds a walkthrough on demand for the specific user in front of it, in real time. Three consequences. Nothing has to be authored : no flow files, no DOM selectors, no quarterly content audits. Nothing breaks when the product changes : ship a feature this morning, move a button this afternoon, and the agent re-learns. Every guide is custom to the user : the agent reads role, account state, and intent before it speaks. Valley cut support tickets 35% and reached time-to-value 3x faster on this model. Frigade also ships Frigade Engage , a code-defined SDK for teams that want to control a specific checklist or banner directly. The two halves work together. Best for SaaS shipping fast enough that authored flows go stale; not the right fit for a single signup flow that hasn't changed in two years. 2. Pendo The analytics incumbent. Pendo 's reason for being is still the data, and it's still good at the data. The guide product was layered on top years later and reads like it. Buyers who run it end-to-end tell us it's fickle: tours pop up in the wrong place, the components look janky, and the janky-ness gets attributed to your product, not to Pendo. It's also heavy. The most consistent complaint we hear from teams considering a switch is load weight and bundle size. The SDK is large, the script adds visible latency to page paint, and customers notice the product feels slower with it on the page. For a tool that's supposed to make your product feel more polished, the math runs the wrong way. If your product team has already standardized on Pendo for analytics, the guide product is the path of least resistance. If you're shopping for guidance specifically, there are tools where guidance is the lead product, not the second one. Pendo's AI features exist; they're roughly what you'd expect from an analytics-led incumbent retrofitting AI onto an author-it-yourself product. Best for mid-to-large product orgs that need analytics and guidance from one vendor and aren't picky about how the guidance feels. 3. WalkMe The original DAP and still the deepest enterprise tool in the category. WalkMe will overlay any web app, including ones you don't own like Salesforce, Workday, or the internal tool from a vendor that hasn't shipped a UI update since 2017. That overlay capability is the whole reason it lives on the IT side of the org as often as the product side. Implementations are measured in months. The buyer it's actually for is the kind of enterprise whose buying timeline is also measured in months: regulated industries, large IT functions, internal rollouts to thousands of employees. Slow is a feature in that buyer profile, not a bug, and WalkMe is priced for it. The tradeoff is brittleness. The author-and-deploy model means a tour is mapped to a specific button, and the moment that button moves, step three breaks. Teams running WalkMe at scale staff a dedicated maintenance function for exactly that reason. WalkMe was acquired by SAP for $1.5B in 2024. The pattern after acquisitions like that is rarely faster innovation; it's slow consolidation into the parent stack. If you're betting on the WalkMe of three years from now to look meaningfully different from the WalkMe of three years ago, we'd take the other side of that bet. 4. Whatfix WalkMe's closest peer. Same enterprise center of gravity, same employee-training tilt, same author-and-redeploy maintenance model. In the bake-offs we've watched, the deciding factor is procurement preference and which customer success team the buyer would be assigned to, not a real architectural difference. Same buyer profile as WalkMe, same caveats about authoring load and breakage on product change. If your evaluation has both vendors on it and you can't articulate why one wins on capability, the evaluation itself is the signal that you're shopping the wrong category. 5. Appcues The original product-led no-code onboarding tool. Mid-market SaaS installs Appcues to ship checklists and tours without an engineering ticket. The editor is mature, the pricing is predictable, the integrations are wide. Our honest read is that Appcues has been the same product for a long time. The calling card has never been quality; the components don't feel native, customization above light theming is painful, and the SDK carries the same performance overhead as the rest of the incumbents on this list. The team has shipped AI features, and they fit the same author-the-flow contract the rest of the product is built on. The category Appcues defined is stable. It is not the category that's growing. Best for SaaS companies that want a simple onboarding stack today and aren't betting on AI displacing the author-it-yourself model in the next renewal cycle. If your product ships often enough that the flows go stale within a quarter, plan for a content function to keep them current or look at the agent-led alternative. 6. Userpilot The modern Appcues, with analytics built in. Lighter on the analytics side than Pendo, more analytics than Appcues, same author-the-flow approach on the guidance side. Strong fit on paper for PLG companies that want one tool covering a funnel they're actively instrumenting. The pattern we see most often with Userpilot is consolidation. Teams that run it alongside Pendo end up killing one of the two within a year because the surfaces overlap too much to justify both budgets. Userpilot inherits the same author-the-flow contract as Appcues and Pendo, which means the same staleness problem at the same cadence. 7. React Joyride (open source) React Joyride is the most widely used React-specific open-source tour library, maintained by Gil Barbara , who's been shipping it solo since 2016. Gil's a good guy and a genuinely talented developer; the library is more thoughtful than the category usually gives him credit for. We started sponsoring React Joyride in 2023. Gil had built the library in the open, and we saw an opportunity to back him: fund more of the work he already enjoyed doing, and put a parallel offer in front of the React developers using it. If you want the tour rendering, take React Joyride. If you want the backend that goes around the tour (state management, segmentation, targeting, eventing, analytics), Frigade Engage is that backend, and you can wire React Joyride into Engage for the rendering layer. Engage offers something React Joyride doesn't, and that complementarity is what made the sponsorship work for both sides. The pick when your stack is React-first and you're not yet ready to pay for the hosted half. Same maintenance contract as the other open-source three. The combination of Engage and React Joyride is its own answer for engineering-led teams that want code-defined onboarding without owning the state layer themselves. 8. Intro.js (open source) Intro.js is the original open-source product tour library, predating the commercial DAP category by years. Dual-licensed: free for non-commercial use, paid license required for commercial use. Lightweight, framework-agnostic, still actively maintained. Shows up most often in internal tools and admin dashboards where a hosted DAP was overkill. Same caveat as the other open-source libraries on this list: you own the content and the breakage. 9. Driver.js (open source) Driver.js is a newer, lightweight tour library focused on highlighting elements and walking users through them. Tiny footprint, zero dependencies, MIT-licensed. We haven't run a production app on it, so we won't pretend to have an opinion beyond that. Same contract as Intro.js: you write the steps, you own the breakage. 10. Shepherd.js (open source) Shepherd.js is the most widely deployed open-source product tour library. MIT-licensed, framework-agnostic, configurable step sequences, themable via CSS. Same fundamental contract as every commercial tour above (author writes the steps, the library renders them), minus the editor, the analytics, and the cohort targeting. If your team is small enough that one engineer owns onboarding and you don't need a hosted authoring experience, it's a defensible pick. The maintenance load is yours, including the brittleness when your DOM changes. How to actually pick The choice in 2026 is binary, and it maps cleanly onto the two halves of this list. Option one: static tours you write and maintain yourself. Pendo, WalkMe, Whatfix, Appcues, and Userpilot are the polished commercial versions of this. React Joyride, Intro.js, Driver.js, and Shepherd are the same model with the license fee removed and the staffing load kept. Sophisticated allocators are running automated scoring models that check for response completeness, flag answer drift across fund vintages, and surface contradictions before anyone on the allocation committee sees the document. If your AI tooling introduces even subtle inconsistencies across submissions, you may be getting eliminated at the algorithmic layer with no feedback and no second chance. This post breaks down how AI is reshaping the fundraising workflow and what your team needs to get it right. TLDR: LP fund close times grew from 14.2 to 18+ months by 2024, and first-time managers face 80%+ rejection rates at screening. Sophisticated LPs now run automated scoring models that can disqualify your DDQ before a human reads it. Generic AI tools fail DDQ workflows by design: probabilistic generation produces inconsistent answers across fund vintages with no flag. Every AI DDQ tool must deliver Accuracy, Consistency, Quality/Customization, and throughput simultaneously; legacy tools cannot hold all four. GovernGPT ingests fund documents autonomously, stores 100+ answer variants per question, and clients report completing RFPs 90-95% faster. The Institutional Fundraising Environment Is Getting Harder to Win The window for institutional capital is narrowing. LP allocations to alternatives have grown more concentrated, with the top quartile of managers capturing a disproportionate share of new commitments. According to Preqin's 2024 Global Private Equity Report , the average time to close a private equity fund increased from 14.2 months in 2021 to over 18 months by 2024, and first-time fund managers face rejection rates exceeding 80% at the initial screening stage. The evaluative bar has risen accordingly. Institutional LPs now run more rigorous structural due diligence, distribute longer and more detailed DDQs, and expect faster turnaround with fewer follow-up cycles. Where AI Is Being Deployed Across the Institutional Fundraising Workflow AI is reshaping institutional fundraising tools at nearly every stage, from initial LP identification through ongoing investor relations. Below are the areas where deployment is most active. Investor Identification and Segmentation Historically, sourcing qualified LPs meant manually cross-referencing allocator databases, conference attendance records, and public filings. AI-assisted tools now parse regulatory filings, mandate disclosures, and portfolio allocation histories to surface investors whose stated criteria align with a fund's strategy before a single call is made. DDQ and RFP Automation Institutional LPs submit DDQs and RFPs that can run hundreds of questions long. AI systems trained on a firm's prior responses, legal documents, and fund materials can draft answers at scale, reducing the time IR teams spend on each DDQ software for investment managers questionnaire. LP Communications and Reporting Quarterly letters, capital call notices, and investor updates increasingly rely on AI to pull performance data, flag reporting inconsistencies, and draft narrative summaries for review. Teams assessing RFP software for hedge funds often start here. Predictive Analytics for Allocation Timing Some GPs now use AI models to analyze macroeconomic indicators, LP liquidity cycles, and prior commitment patterns to identify optimal windows for re-engagement or follow-on conversations. Compliance Monitoring Regulatory filings, marketing materials, and LP-facing communications require ongoing review against SEC, CFTC, and applicable international standards. AI-assisted compliance tools flag language that may require legal review before distribution. The DDQ and RFP Burden Is Compounding The volume of DDQs and RFPs hitting institutional fundraising teams has grown sharply over the past several years. According to Preqin, the average LP now submits between 50 and 150 detailed questions per DDQ cycle, and GPs managing multiple fund vintages often field hundreds of overlapping requests simultaneously. The problem is not the volume alone. It is that each questionnaire arrives with its own formatting requirements, scoring criteria, and LP-specific language expectations, and the cost of a generic or inconsistent response is no longer just a wasted hour of analyst time. Sophisticated LPs are deploying automated scoring models that grade response completeness, flag answer inconsistencies across prior fund filings, and surface contradictions before a human reviewer opens the document. A GP whose answers subtly contradict a prior filing can be eliminated before reaching the allocation committee, with no human ever having read the submission. That is the operating environment. DDQ quality is now a competitive survival requirement, not an administrative function. Why Generic AI Tools Cannot Handle Institutional DDQ at Quality The problem with off-the-shelf AI in institutional DDQ workflows is architectural, not cosmetic. Every general-purpose LLM operates on probabilistic generation: it samples from a distribution of possible outputs instead of retrieving from a controlled, version-specific answer set. Ask the same fee structure question twice across two analysts or two fund vintages, and AI hallucination in fund manager DDQs may produce materially different answers, with no flag, no conflict alert, and no human noticing the discrepancy. The first reader to catch it may be an LP's automated scoring model. That failure cannot be patched with better prompts. The inconsistency lives in the data architecture, not the generation layer. A model built to retrieve from a single, version-controlled answer set cannot produce a variant it was never shown. A model with no such boundary cannot guarantee it won't. The same architectural gap that produces inconsistency also produces the more dangerous failure: subtle inaccuracy. General-purpose LLMs are built to satisfy instructions, which means they will generate a plausible-sounding answer even when the underlying verified data is unavailable. In a DDQ context, this manifests not as obvious fabrication but as wrong fund figures, outdated performance data, or language that sounds authoritative while silently contradicting a prior LP communication. The nuance is the risk: IR reviewers are trained to assess tone and completeness, not to audit individual data points against source documents. A fluent, well-structured answer that contains a stale figure from a prior fund vintage will pass that review. The LP's automated scoring model may catch it. GovernGPT tackles this at the source: approximately 90% of pre-population is drawn from verbatim pre-approved content with full traceability, and any AI-generated bridge sentences are explicitly flagged for reviewer attention, so reviewers know exactly what to verify instead of reviewing everything or nothing. What Generic Tools Get Wrong at the Data Layer Most off-the-shelf tools compound the generation problem with a data problem: Ingestion is manual and lossy, requiring analyst hours before the system can produce any output, which means the library reflects whoever last touched it, not current fund reality. Storage cannot accommodate answer variation at scale. At 200 Q&A entries, a loosely tagged library is workable. At 2,500, the same taxonomy returns 30 to 40 results per query with no ranking by fund vintage or LP type, and analysts stop trusting the system entirely. Retrieval is static, meaning the system surfaces the closest textual match, never the contextually correct answer for a specific LP mandate, fund vehicle, or regulatory environment. These are not feature gaps. They are load-bearing design decisions that make accuracy structurally impossible. There is also a keyman risk dimension that compounds the decay: when the analyst who built and maintained the tag taxonomy leaves, the institutional knowledge encoded in those tags leaves with them. Tags break, entries go stale, and the library continues returning results, with no signal that the output is no longer current. GovernGPT eliminates this failure mode by autonomously ingesting, tagging, and maintaining fund documents without any human-maintained taxonomy. The knowledge base is encoded in architecture, not in any individual's head. The Four Outcomes an AI DDQ Solution Must Deliver Simultaneously Four outcomes define whether an AI DDQ solution actually works in production: Accuracy, Consistency, Quality/Customization, and Throughput. Legacy tools could never deliver all four simultaneously. That is not a feature gap; it is an architectural one. Why All Four Must Coexist Most IR teams that have trialed tools covered in any DDQ software comparison for asset managers find they can get speed, or they can get coverage, but not both without sacrificing accuracy. Here is what each outcome requires and why they cannot be solved in isolation: Outcome What It Requires What Failure Looks Like Accuracy Every answer reflects current fund data at the vehicle level Blended retrieval that cannot distinguish Fund III from Fund IV Consistency The same question returns the same answer across analysts and fund vintages, with no version drift and no silent contradictions Two analysts query the same fee structure question and receive materially different answers with no flag Quality / Customization Responses calibrated to the specific mandate of the receiving allocator (ESG frameworks, Solvency II, infrastructure-weighted criteria) A public pension fund with an ESG mandate reads a generic risk answer as a disqualifying signal, not a neutral one Throughput High acceptance rate (the percentage of AI-generated answers usable without editing) Output requiring heavy revision adds review burden; clients report completing RFPs 90 to 95% faster with GovernGPT The failure mode of every legacy tool is that optimizing for one outcome degrades another. Speed without a controlled data architecture produces inaccurate output. Coverage without version control produces inconsistency. Any solution that cannot hold all four simultaneously has not solved the problem. AI Governance and Compliance Controls in LP Communications As AI-generated content moves deeper into LP communications, governance and compliance controls have shifted from optional to expected. The SEC's guidance on AI in investment management makes clear that material inconsistencies in fund disclosures constitute regulatory violations regardless of whether a human or an AI produced them, making AI compliance review tools for asset managers a critical layer of defense. If an answer goes out, the firm owns the liability. For IR teams, every AI-assisted DDQ response requires a defensible audit trail: who approved it, which source document it was drawn from, and when that source was last verified. Without that chain, stale DDQ content risk from a prior fund vintage becomes a material misstatement. No human reviewer can reliably catch every variant across hundreds of LP submissions under deadline pressure. Governance architecture must be baked into the tooling itself, not retrofitted through manual review. That means the AI must be a glassbox, not a blackbox: one that writes like tier-1 funds' best RFP authors, draws only from verbatim pre-approved content wherever that content exists, uses AI only to bridge gaps in existing approved language, and makes every sourcing decision fully traceable. When compliance teams cannot see which line came from a source document and which was generated by the model, they cannot sign off on the output with confidence, and an output that cannot be formally approved has not solved the compliance problem, regardless of how fluent it reads. LP-Side Automated Scoring and the Algorithmic Disqualification Risk The first reviewer of your DDQ submission may not be a human. Sophisticated LPs are deploying automated scoring models that grade response completeness, flag answer inconsistencies across prior fund filings, and surface contradictions before anyone on the allocation committee opens the document. A GP whose answers subtly contradict a prior filing can be eliminated at the algorithmic layer, with no human ever having read the submission. This is the current operating environment for institutional capital allocation. What Automated LP Scoring Actually Measures These systems do not read for narrative quality. They score across three dimensions: Response completeness against a predefined question taxonomy, where missing sub-answers register as gaps regardless of prose quality elsewhere in the document Cross-vintage consistency, where the scoring model compares current answers against prior fund filings and flags deviations above a defined tolerance threshold LP-specific calibration, where responses are checked for acknowledgment of the LP's stated mandate, such as ESG frameworks, Solvency II constraints, or infrastructure-weighted allocation criteria A response that reads well to a human reviewer can still fail all three of these checks algorithmically. Fluency is not a scoring input. The capital consequence is direct: a GP eliminated before the allocation committee stage loses the relationship without ever receiving feedback, because the automated system does not generate rejection rationale a human would think to share. How to Vet AI Tools Built for Institutional Fundraising Before committing to any AI tool for institutional fundraising workflows, vetting DDQ software matters as much as the vendor demo. A tool that performs well in a controlled demo environment and fails under a live DDQ deadline is not a tool that adds capacity; it is a liability. Start with acceptance rate. What percentage of AI-generated answers can your IR team send without editing? A low acceptance rate means the tool adds review burden instead of removing it, making it a net negative on analyst time. Any vendor that cannot cite this number has implicitly answered the question. Then audit the data architecture: Does the system ingest documents autonomously, or does setup require your team to pre-clean and reformat source files before the tool can process them? Ingestion overhead in a POC is not a setup cost; it is a preview of production. Can it store 100+ answer variants at the vehicle level, or does it blend the closest available match when a specific variant does not exist? Does it track answer variation across fund vintages, or will two analysts querying the same question on different days retrieve materially different answers with no flag? Finally, ask whether the tool writes like IR writes, drawing from the latest pre-approved content, or whether it generates probabilistically from a document corpus it has never been disciplined to control. For teams focused on winning LP capital in institutional fundraising across multiple vehicles, that throughput difference is the margin between winning an allocation and missing a deadline. body_text: Nature Human Behaviour study finds SilverCloud® by Amwell® reduced prevalence of mental disorders over two years at scale May 18, 2026 PDF Version BOSTON, May 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Amwell ® (NYSE: AMWL), a leading provider of a comprehensive SaaS-based software platform for technology-enabled healthcare, today highlighted results from an independently led, National Institute of Mental Health-funded randomized trial published in Nature Human Behaviour examining SilverCloud® by Amwell ® , the company’s digital behavioral health solution. Conducted across 26 U.S. colleges and universities , the study included 6,205 students at clinical or high-risk levels for anxiety, depression, and/or eating disorders , making it one of the largest independent studies of its kind. The study, led by renowned investigators from Washington University, Penn State University and University of California, Los Angeles, used a proactive care model designed to reach students before conditions worsened. Researchers screened nearly 40,000 students and offered support to those identified as being at elevated risk, rather than relying only on traditional pathways that require students to seek care on their own. Principal Investigator Michelle G. Newman, PhD, Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry, Penn State University shares her insights on the study: "Our goal was early detection of those at risk or meeting clinical levels for five mental health conditions, and to test whether digital mental health could move care upstream — reaching people earlier, before symptoms worsen, and doing so at population scale .” Individuals offered SilverCloud were over twice as likely to engage: 74.4% participation with SilverCloud 30.2% participation with traditional behavioral health solutions Compared to screening and referral to in-person care, those who received digital behavioral healthcare had: 4.3% lower prevalence of having any mental disorder at six weeks 4.9% lower prevalence at six months 3.8% lower prevalence at two years This positive impact was consistent across student populations, including minoritized students and those experiencing financial stress. The findings also point to the potential economic value of prevention and earlier intervention at scale. When asked about the impact of the study, co-investigator Daniel Eisenberg, PhD, Health Economist, Professor of Health Policy and Management, UCLA said, “The findings suggest meaningful potential economic value . By combining proactive outreach with a structured digital intervention, the study points to a model that may help address both participation and long-term outcomes in populations with significant unmet need. title: Cold Email Subject Lines That Actually Convert (2026 Data)
summary: What subject line length, format, and tone gets the highest open and reply rates? Data from real B2B cold email campaigns — not recycled '10 best' listicles.
body_text: What is the best cold email subject line length? 4–7 words. Subject lines in this range have 15–20% higher open rates than longer alternatives. They display fully on mobile (where 60%+ of B2B email is first seen) and feel personal rather than promotional. Should I use the recipient's name in the subject line? It depends on the context. A first name alone ('Ayush') can work if the rest of the email is genuinely personalized. But {{First_Name}} in the subject line of a clearly templated email signals 'mass outreach' and hurts more than it helps. Do emojis work in cold email subject lines? For B2B cold email to mid-market and enterprise: no. Emoji subject lines correlate with 10–15% lower open rates in our data. They signal consumer marketing, not professional outreach. Should I A/B test subject lines? Yes, but only if you're sending enough volume for the test to be statistically meaningful. Below 200 emails per variant, the data is noise. Above 500, patterns become reliable.

title: SA-2026-048 - ExtremeCloud IQ Cross-Tenant Data Exposure via Extreme Platform One Authentication Race Condition (CVE-2026-9831)
summary: A race condition in the shared Extreme Platform ONE IAM Gateway API-key authentication path could, under specific high-concurrency traffic conditions, intermittently allow requests authenticated with an Extreme Platform ONE/IAM-issued API key to receive response data for another tenant. The issue was observed through ExtremeCloud IQ/XIQ API endpoints and validated against both XIQ/XAPI and Extreme Platform ONE/Common Services API paths. XIQ-native tokens and standard OAuth/Bearer JWT authentication were not affected. Extreme Networks thanks Sebastian Koller of Iteas IT Services GmbH for the responsible disclosure of this issue. Furthermore, products that have exceeded any software maintenance time periods are also not evaluated and will not be published. Net Income decreased to $37.7 million from $44.2 million in the prior year. These decreases were partially offset by an increase in other income due primarily to fair value adjustments of financial instruments and lower interest expense. Net Debt and Net Leverage as of March 31, 2026 was $657.1 million and 1.7x, respectively. Share Repurchase Program During the quarter, we repurchased 306,570 shares at an average price of $15.13 per share, totaling $4.6 million. $95.4 million remained available for repurchase under the share repurchase program. Outlook for Fiscal Year 2026 (forward-looking statement) We are pleased with the solid start to the year and the positive momentum we are seeing across our operations. Conditions in the Middle East continue to evolve, resulting in a more complex operating environment and directly impacting on our cost base. We anticipate increased shipping and fuel costs in the second quarter, particularly in our Fresh Fruit segment. However, as the year progresses, we expect to see the benefit of contract price adjustments, as well as the benefit of our dynamic pricing strategy in our diversified divisions, coming through. We believe that our resilient and diversified business model positions us well to handle today's complex environment. Alongside this, demand for our products remains strong, supported by prevailing health and wellness trends. We also anticipate positive returns from our recent investments and remain committed to advancing our development pipeline. Considering all relevant factors, we are maintaining our target of a full-year Adjusted EBITDA of at least $400 million for 2026. We are maintaining our guidance for routine capex of approximately $100 million. In addition, we continue to explore a range of development opportunities which, if executed, will strengthen our business and continue to drive further growth in the years to come. Adjusted EBITDA is calculated from GAAP net income by: (1) subtracting the income or adding the loss from discontinued operations, net of income taxes; (2) adding the income tax expense or subtracting the income tax benefit; (3) adding interest expense; (4) adding depreciation charges; (5) adding amortization charges on intangible assets; (6) adding mark to market losses or subtracting mark to market gains related to unrealized impacts from certain derivative instruments and foreign currency denominated borrowings, realized impacts on noncash settled foreign currency denominated borrowings, net foreign currency impacts on liquidated entities and fair value movements on contingent consideration; (7) other items which are separately stated based on materiality, which during the three months ended March 31, 2026 and March 31, 2025, included subtracting the gain or adding the loss on the disposal of business interests, subtracting the gain or adding the loss on asset sales for assets held for sale and actively marketed property or sales-type leases, adding impairment charges or held for sale classification losses on property, plant and equipment and lease assets, subtracting interest income on deferred transaction consideration, adding acquisition and transaction costs and adding restructuring charges and costs for legal matters not in the ordinary course of business; and (8) the Company’s share of these items from equity method investments. LTM Adjusted EBITDA for the year ended December 31, 2025 is the same as Adjusted EBITDA for the year ended December 31, 2025. Adjusted Net Income is calculated from GAAP net income attributable to Dole plc by: (1) subtracting the income or adding the loss from discontinued operations, net of income taxes; (2) adding amortization charges on intangible assets; (3) adding mark to market losses or subtracting mark to market gains related to unrealized impacts from certain derivative instruments and foreign currency denominated borrowings, realized impacts on noncash settled foreign currency denominated borrowings, net foreign currency impacts on liquidated entities and fair value movements on contingent consideration; (4) other items which are separately stated based on materiality, which during the three months ended March 31, 2026 and March 31, 2025, included subtracting the gain or adding the loss on the disposal of business interests, subtracting the gain or adding the loss on asset sales for assets held for sale and actively marketed property or sales-type leases, adding impairment charges or held for sale classification losses on property, plant and equipment and lease assets, adding acquisition and transaction costs and adding restructuring charges and costs for legal matters not in the ordinary course of business; (5) the Company’s share of these items from equity method investments; (6) excluding the tax effect of these items and discrete tax adjustments; and (7) excluding the effect of these items attributable to non-controlling interests. Adjusted Earnings per Share is calculated from Adjusted Net Income divided by diluted weighted average number of shares in the applicable period. Net Debt is a non-GAAP financial measure, calculated as GAAP cash and cash equivalents, less GAAP current and long-term debt. It also excludes GAAP unamortized debt discounts and debt issuance costs. Net Leverage is a non-GAAP financial measure, calculated as Net Debt divided by LTM Adjusted EBITDA, both of which are defined above. Free cash flow from continuing operations is calculated from GAAP net cash used in or provided by operating activities for continuing operations less GAAP capital expenditures. Like-for-like basis refers to the U.S. GAAP measure or non-GAAP financial measure excluding the impact of foreign currency translation movements and acquisitions and divestitures. The impact of foreign currency translation represents an estimate of the effect of translating the results of operations denominated in a foreign currency to U.S. Dollar at prior year average rates, as compared to current year average rates.
